newsitem.title: USA: Potential fat drug may have diabetes link.
newsitem.headline: Potential fat drug may have diabetes link.

text.p: The protein leptin, regarded as a potential fat-buster, might aggravate diabetes or create diabetes-like symptoms, a factor that would have to be taken into account if it is developed into a weight-loss drug, an Israeli scientist reported Thursday.

A separate researcher at the National Institutes of Health said the finding should be a factor in leptin research but should not derail the research effort, mostly conducted by biotech company Amgen Inc.

An Amgen spokesman was not immediately available for comment. Leptin was discovered two years ago at Rockefeller University and has been shown to cause weight-loss in mice. There are many unanswered questions about how it works in humans.

Israeli scientist Menachem Rubinstein of the Weizmann Institute of Science reports in Friday's edition of the journal Science that high levels of leptin disrupt some activities of insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar levels.
However his research was based on liver cell samples, and the same effects might not be seen in humans who have leptin receptors in several organs.
Rubinstein also wrote that his finding may also help teach scientists more about the causes of diabetes.

National Institutes of Health researcher Simeon Taylor, who wrote an accompanying article in the journal, said in a telephone interview that drug developers would have to pay attention to the glucose levels of people in clinical trials, but that the finding was not an insurmountable obstacle to drug development.

Losing weight has health effects, including lowering glucose, that might cancel out any effect leptin has on raising it, he said. Or leptin could prove to have side effects in some people which would have to be monitored the same way patients taking numerous other drugs are watched, he said.
"The clinical trials are under way and I think until they are done, no one will know the answers," he said.
"It's a major extrapolation from the test tube to the patient," he said. "Time will tell."
